title: Stormbridge — Proxy Stack Evaluation
summary: Initial technical evaluation focused on integrating Redwood behind Stormbridge's API gateway/proxy. Key concerns: VPC connectivity, rate limits/quotas across teams, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter compatibility, observability hooks, and deciding between hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment. Agreed to run a small pilot with SDK examples and a throughput benchmark.
topics: Rate limits, quotas and tenant isolation
Observability hooks: traces, metrics, token-level cost
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Priya Menon: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Priya, AE at Redwood Inference. With me is Alex Chen, our systems SE — Alex do you want to wave hi?
[00:08] Alex Chen: Hey, hi.
[00:11] Dana Ruiz: Hi Priya, Alex. Dana here. Good to meet you. We're excited to see how Redwood fits into our pipeline.
[00:18] Marcus Ellison: Marcus from platform — we run a proxy layer in front of all model calls so curious how that'll behave.
[00:24] Leah Park: Leah, SRE, focused on quotas, burst policy, and observability.
[00:29] Priya Menon: Awesome, quick agenda — we wanted to understand Stormbridge's proxy/gateway stack, constraints, then talk SDKs and LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, and then next steps for a pilot. Sound OK?
[00:40] Dana Ruiz: Yep. We'll start with our current stack — we put a Kong-based gateway in front of microservices, plus an Envoy sidecar on every pod. All model calls currently go through an internal proxy to enforce quotas and routing.
[00:53] Marcus Ellison: We also have multi-tenant quotas — product teams have soft quotas and we throttle at the proxy layer. Latency budget is tight: p50 under 120ms for our chat features, p95 under 350ms.
[01:05] Alex Chen: Quick clarifying question — when you say proxy do you enforce token-level accounting at the proxy or just request counting?
[01:12] Marcus Ellison: Today it's request-level. We've been debating moving to token-level billing but it's complex in our stack because we chunk and stream.
[01:19] Alex Chen: Got it. Redwood has token accounting at the API level and can stream back partial tokens. For hosted it's straightforward; with a proxy you want to pass X-Request-ID and have traceability so cost attribution works end-to-end.
[01:32] Leah Park: Do you have SDKs we can run inside the proxy or do we need to call Redwood directly?
[01:37] Priya Menon: We provide language SDKs and a light client that can be embedded in services. For sidecars you can use the SDK to call Redwood or route via your gateway to the hosted endpoint — both patterns are used. Alex, do you want to explain the sidecar vs gateway tradeoffs?
[01:50] Alex Chen: Sure. Sidecar/local calls minimize network hops and let you keep KV cache closer to the app (prefix caching), which helps latency. Gateway centralizes routing and quota policy but adds a hop. With dedicated capacity you can colocate and reduce network egress for private deployments.
[02:05] Dana Ruiz: We're evaluating hosted first for speed of integration, but security and data controls are also major. We need SOC 2 type 2, SSO/SAML, and ability to integrate our KMS for at-rest keys.
[02:15] Priya Menon: Hosted supports SOC 2, SSO via SAML, and we have KMS integrations for private deployments. For strict key control you can choose Private where customer manages keys.
[02:24] Marcus Ellison: If we move to Private, can we keep the same SDKs we use for hosted?
[02:28] Alex Chen: Yes — same API surface. The deployment abstraction is consistent: same endpoints and SDKs, different routing and auth. Small differences in network configuration and some plugin setup for on-prem.
[02:38] Leah Park: Observability — what do you emit? We need traces, per-request token counts and cost, and logs we can ship to our ELK.
[02:46] Alex Chen: We emit request traces, token-level breakdowns, latency histograms, and optional structured audit logs. You can stream metrics to Prometheus and ship logs to your ELK via our log-forwarder.
[02:56] Priya Menon: Also our Console shows per-route token cost and model-level latency breakdowns — helpful for teams to see hot prompt patterns.
[03:05] Marcus Ellison: How mature is LangChain and LlamaIndex support? Our engineering team uses both in internal tooling.
[03:11] Alex Chen: We have first-class LangChain adapters and a maintained LlamaIndex connector in our SDK repo. They support streaming and function/tool calling. Caveat: sometimes library versions drift, so we recommend pinning to the adapter version we provide.
[03:23] Dana Ruiz: Do you provide example apps that show embedding pipelines + retrieval + reranking?
[03:29] Priya Menon: Yes — we have a samples repo: embedding-pipeline-examples and a retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) starter. I'll share links after the call.
[03:36] Marcus Ellison: On quotas, we need per-team quotas and emergency overrides. Can Redwood enforce that?
[03:43] Alex Chen: You can create API keys scoped to projects with quota limits, and our routing layer supports policy-based overrides — e.g., allowlist for emergency requests. If you front with your own proxy you can also enforce additional constraints at your side.
[03:55] Leah Park: Rate-limiting under burst — we sometimes get traffic spikes of 3x baseline. Does Redwood provide burst capacity or graceful degradation?
[04:02] Priya Menon: Dedicated pools have configurable burst capacity and SLO-backed throughput; hosted has soft burst options. There are automatic fallbacks to smaller model variants if capacity is constrained, configured by routing policies.
[04:16] Dana Ruiz: Hmm — can you explain the fallback logic for model variants? We don't want big regressions in quality.
[04:21] Alex Chen: Fallbacks are by policy — you map primary model to compatible smaller variant and define acceptance thresholds. Also you can set canary rollouts and A/B tests so you can monitor quality regressions with eval prompt sets.
[04:34] Marcus Ellison: We're concerned about streaming through the proxy: does Redwood support chunked streaming and how does that affect proxy timeouts?
[04:41] Alex Chen: We support streaming (SSE/websocket) and recommend your proxy extend the timeout for streaming routes. Alternatively you can terminate the stream at the proxy and forward to backend but that loses native streaming semantics.
[04:55] Leah Park: Security question — audit logs must be tamper-evident for compliance. Is that possible?
[05:01] Priya Menon: For Private deployments we can enable audit log hashing and forward to your SIEM. Hosted audit trails are stored and can be exported; for highest assurance we recommend Private with customer-managed keying for logs.
[05:12] Dana Ruiz: Good to know. Next, SDK ergonomics: our developers use TypeScript and Python. Are both first-class?
[05:18] Alex Chen: Yes — TS and Python SDKs, plus a lightweight HTTP client. We have example LangChain wrappers in TS and Python.
[05:25] Marcus Ellison: Can the SDK run inside our Envoy filter or would you recommend calling Redwood from a sidecar process?
[05:31] Alex Chen: Calling from sidecar is usually simpler — avoids pushing heavy SDK logic into the filter. If you prefer filter-level enforcement we have a small HTTP shim you can call from filters.
[05:41] Leah Park: For billing we need to attribute spend to teams — does the SDK pass metadata for internal billing?
[05:47] Priya Menon: You can send metadata headers (team-id, project-id). We have cost attribution tooling that surfaces that in the Console.
[05:54] Dana Ruiz: Ok, what does a pilot look like?
[05:57] Priya Menon: Typically a 2–3 week pilot: Redwood provides a sandbox API key, SDK samples, and a small benchmark harness. We help run throughput tests, a correctness eval on a prompt set, and measure latency/cost.
[06:08] Marcus Ellison: Measurement details — we want to simulate 1k concurrent short-chat requests and a RAG path with embedding lookups.
[06:15] Alex Chen: We can instrument a benchmark that simulates your split: 70% chat, 30% RAG; include embedding requests and simulate 2k doc retrievals to exercise KV and cache.
[06:25] Leah Park: Would you need access to production data? We prefer synthetic.
[06:28] Priya Menon: Synthetic is fine; if you want fidelity we can hash or redact live data.
[06:33] Dana Ruiz: Any limitations on model size or sequence length? We often have 2k token contexts for RAG.
[06:39] Alex Chen: Our runtime supports long contexts; kernel selection will vary. For 2k sequences we recommend a quantized model profile to keep latency lower on dedicated pools.
[06:49] Marcus Ellison: What about self-hosting in our VPC — how much ops work?
[06:54] Priya Menon: For Private VPC there's an installer and orchestration; it'll take collaboration with your infra team — typically a few weeks for basic setup, longer for air-gapped on-prem. We'll provide runbooks.
[07:05] Dana Ruiz: Cost question: how predictable is pricing if we go hosted vs dedicated?
[07:09] Priya Menon: Hosted is usage-based (per token/embedding). Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly commit — more predictable and often cheaper at scale. Private has licensing plus infra costs. We'll share a pricing sketch.
[07:19] Leah Park: Competitors — are other customers moving to Redwood from OpenAI or internal models and why?
[07:25] Priya Menon: Common reasons: control over latency/cost at scale, better routing/fallbacks, and unified tooling across on-prem and cloud. Some teams use Redwood as a gateway to multiple model providers, including Anthropic and OpenAI, depending on policy.
[07:40] Marcus Ellison: For our team, the biggest blockers are latency under our proxy and token accounting per team. If you can show a sample with token attribution and p95 under 350ms in our benchmark, we'd be in good shape.
[07:53] Alex Chen: Understood. We'll prepare an integration plan: share SDK examples, a LangChain adapter sample, and a benchmark harness.
[07:59] Dana Ruiz: Timeline — we'd like a pilot next sprint (start 2026-09-06) if possible.
[08:04] Priya Menon: That works on our side — Alex, can we commit to deliverables?
[08:09] Alex Chen: Yes. I'll assemble a repo with sample code (TS + Python), a LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter example, and a benchmark script.
[08:19] Leah Park: When we ran a quick test internally with our proxy, we saw timeouts around 30s for streaming routes — we'll include our proxy timeout configs.
[08:26] Marcus Ellison: Also, we need RBAC around keys — only platform can create keys, apps get scoped keys.
[08:31] Priya Menon: RBAC and API key scoping supported; we can map to your identity provider for SSO/SAML.
[08:37] Dana Ruiz: Any docs or security questionnaires we should review?
[08:41] Priya Menon: I'll share our security pack (SOC 2 report, encryption whitepaper) and a technical integration doc.
[08:48] Alex Chen: One more technical note — if you're using prefix caching at the KV level, we recommend configuring cache TTL aligned with embedding freshness to avoid stale retrievals.
[08:58] Marcus Ellison: Good call.
[09:00] Priya Menon: Alright let's do a quick recap — next steps and owners.
[09:05] Dana Ruiz: Thanks everyone.
[09:07] [END OF TRANSCRIPT — meeting lasted ~42 minutes]
next_steps: Priya to send security pack (SOC 2, encryption whitepaper) and example repos by 2026-09-02
Alex to share SDK + LangChain + LlamaIndex sample repo and benchmark harness by 2026-09-03
Stormbridge to provide proxy timeout configs and a small synthetic dataset by 2026-09-04
Schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2026-09-06 (tentative)

Priya Menon: share security pack and pricing sketch (due 2026-09-02)
